/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

Biologics are one group of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, or DMARDs. Conventional DMARDs, biological DMARDs and targeted synthetic DMARDs work in different ways. Treatment depends on the diagnosis, disease activity, previous treatment and safety checks. A rheumatology team decides which approach is appropriate with you.

Conventional DMARDs

For rheumatoid arthritis, medicines such as methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine can reduce the inflammatory disease process. They are different from painkillers. The choice and monitoring plan are individual; some people need more than one medicine.

Biological DMARDs

Examples include adalimumab and etanercept. Biological treatment may be considered when conventional treatment has not controlled rheumatoid arthritis adequately, subject to the relevant NICE criteria. These medicines are given by injection or infusion, depending on the product. They may be used alongside another DMARD.

Where JAK inhibitors fit

JAK inhibitors are targeted synthetic DMARDs, not biological DMARDs. They are another specialist treatment option for some people with rheumatoid arthritis when other treatment is unsuitable or has not worked well enough. Eligibility and risks need an individual discussion.

Why the diagnosis matters

Treatment for rheumatoid arthritis cannot simply be copied to axial spondyloarthritis. NHS guidance says conventional DMARDs may help inflammation in joints outside the spine but do not treat spinal symptoms. Axial disease has its own exercise, physiotherapy and medicine pathway under NICE NG65.

Questions for your team

Ask what the treatment is intended to change, how response will be measured, which tests and vaccinations are needed, and who to contact about possible infection or side effects. Do not change doses or pause treatment using a general comparison article. Follow your own team and product information.

/resources/flare-action-plan.answer: An arthritis flare-up action plan is a written plan you make while you are well, so you know what to do when a flare starts: your usual and flare signs, gentle self-care steps, medicines your own clinicians have agreed, who to contact, and the red flag signs that mean you need urgent help. Print the free plan below and fill it in.
/resources/flare-action-plan.bodyHtml:
Editorial update: 22 November 2026. This editorial safety update is not independent clinical review.

What an arthritis flare-up action plan is

A flare-up action plan is a short written plan you make while you feel reasonably well, so that you are not trying to make decisions when pain is at its worst. It tells you what to do in the first hours and days of a flare, which medicines your own clinicians have agreed you can use, who to call, and which warning signs mean you need urgent help instead of self-care.

Many people with arthritis find that a flare is not only painful but unsettling. It can be hard to think clearly, remember what helped last time or know whether to ring the GP. A plan on paper takes that pressure off. It is also useful for a partner, family member or carer, who can follow it with you.

This page gives you a ready-made plan to print and fill in. It works for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout and other types, but the details you write in should come from your own GP, rheumatology team, pharmacist or physiotherapist. It is educational information, not a personal treatment plan.

Why writing a plan in advance helps

Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) suggests that people plan for flares ahead of time, including knowing what to do and who to contact. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) also says people should have access to a named contact in their specialist team and rapid access to advice when symptoms flare. A written plan turns that advice into something you can actually use on a bad day.

  • You act sooner. Starting gentle self-care early often makes a flare easier to manage than waiting to see if it settles.
  • You avoid guessing with medicines. You write down only what your clinician or pharmacist has agreed, including maximum doses.
  • You know when to stop self-care. Red flag signs are written on the same page, so they are hard to miss.
  • Appointments are more useful. Bringing your notes helps your GP or specialist team see patterns and adjust treatment.
  • Other people can help. A carer or family member can follow the same steps.

How to fill in your plan: step by step

  1. Print the plan below (use the Print button at the top of the page, or your browser's print option). You can also save it as a PDF from the print window and keep it on your phone.
  2. Describe what your flares usually look like. Which joints, what the pain feels like, whether there is swelling, warmth, stiffness or tiredness. This helps you tell a flare from an ordinary bad day.
  3. Write your green, amber and red signs. Use the zone table. Green is your usual day. Amber is a flare you can manage at home. Red means get medical help.
  4. Take the medicines section to your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology nurse. Ask them to agree what you can use during a flare, at what dose and for how long. Do not fill this in from memory or from the internet.
  5. Add your contacts. GP surgery, rheumatology advice line if you have one, community pharmacy, physiotherapist, and a friend or relative who can help.
  6. Choose your comfort steps. Heat, cold, gentle movement, rest positions and pacing ideas that have helped you before.
  7. Keep it somewhere obvious. On the fridge, by the bed, in your bag or as a photo on your phone. Tell the people close to you where it is.
  8. Review it after each flare and at least once a year, or whenever your medicines change.

Fill this in with a pen. Bring it to your next GP, rheumatology or physiotherapy appointment.

Filling in the zones: what to think about

Green zone: your usual day

Your green zone is your normal, which may still include some pain. Writing down a typical pain score and how long morning stiffness usually lasts gives you a baseline to compare against. People with osteoarthritis often have stiffness that eases within about half an hour, while inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis often causes longer morning stiffness. Your own baseline matters more than any general rule.

Green-zone habits are what make flares less likely or less severe: regular exercise suited to you, pacing, a healthy weight, good sleep routines and taking regular medicines as prescribed. NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) puts tailored exercise and, where relevant, weight management at the centre of care.

Amber zone: a flare you can manage at home

Amber is a flare that feels familiar. It is worse than usual, but you recognise it and you have no red flag signs. Common features are more pain for more than a day, extra stiffness, some swelling, poorer sleep and more tiredness. Your plan should say what you will do and, importantly, how long you will manage it yourself before asking for advice. Ask your clinician what that timescale should be for you, because it depends on your type of arthritis and treatment.

Red zone: get medical help

Red means something may be different from your usual arthritis, or you may be unwell for another reason. Seek urgent GP or urgent-care advice for severe joint pain that started suddenly, usually in one joint. Swelling around a joint, changed skin colour or difficulty moving the joint also need urgent advice. Joint pain with fever, shivering or feeling unwell also needs urgent advice. These signs do not all need to occur together. Do not wait for a fever. Use 111 where available, or your local urgent-care route in Northern Ireland. Call 999 for life-threatening symptoms. Fever is not always present with a joint infection. Follow the emergency routes in Part 5 for emergency warning signs; do not wait for non-emergency advice.

Comfort steps that commonly help during a flare

  • Short rest, not bed rest. Resting a very painful joint for a short time is reasonable, but long periods without moving tend to increase stiffness and weakness. Small, gentle movements through a comfortable range every hour or so while awake usually help.
  • Cold for hot joints. A bag of frozen peas or a cold pack wrapped in a tea towel, for around 10 to 15 minutes at a time. Avoid cold on numb skin or if you have Raynaud's phenomenon and it triggers symptoms.
  • Warmth for stiff joints. A warm shower, wheat bag or hot water bottle in a cover, for around 15 to 20 minutes. Check your skin often and never use heat on numb skin or a hot, swollen joint.
  • Pacing. Break tasks into smaller pieces with rests in between, and drop or delegate what you can for a few days. Our pacing and energy guide explains how.
  • Joint protection. Use gadgets, bigger grips, trolleys and bags with straps to take strain off painful joints. See our joint protection guide.
  • Sleep set-up. Pillows to support sore joints and a regular bedtime routine. A flare often disturbs sleep, and poor sleep makes pain harder to cope with.
  • Mind and mood. Breathing exercises, relaxation, gentle distraction and talking to someone you trust. It is normal to feel low or frustrated during a flare.

Medicines: what to agree with your clinician

Medicines are the part of the plan you should never improvise. What is safe depends on your age, kidneys, stomach, heart, blood pressure, other medicines and type of arthritis. A pharmacist can check over-the-counter options, and your GP or rheumatology team can agree anything stronger.

  • Osteoarthritis: NICE NG226 recommends considering a topical anti-inflammatory gel for knee osteoarthritis first, and for other joints it may also help. If anti-inflammatory tablets are needed, NICE advises the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with stomach protection. NICE does not recommend paracetamol or weak opioids as routine treatment for osteoarthritis.
  • Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis: your specialist team may agree a flare plan, which can include a short course or injection of steroids or a change to your regular treatment. Ask how to contact them and how quickly they want to hear from you. NICE NG100 supports rapid access to specialist advice for flares.
  • Gout: NICE's gout guideline (NG219) covers treatments for a gout flare. If you have been given a flare treatment, write down exactly how to take it.
  • Steroids: if you take steroid tablets regularly, you may need a steroid emergency card, and you should not stop them suddenly. Read our guide to steroid emergency cards.

After the flare: review your plan

When things settle, spend ten minutes looking back. What started it, if you can tell? What helped most? Did anything make it worse? How long did it last? Did you need help sooner than you thought? Update your plan, and bring your tracking table to your next appointment. If flares are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe, that is worth discussing with your GP or specialist team, because your treatment may need reviewing.

After a long flare, it is common to feel weaker and less fit. Build activity back up gradually rather than jumping straight back to your old routine. Our guide to getting moving again after a flare can help.

When to get medical help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, signs of a stroke, collapse, or sudden loss of vision.
  • Back pain with new neurological warning signs: If you have back pain with new bladder or bowel changes, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, call 999 or go to A&E immediately. Do not drive yourself.
  • Sudden severe joint pain or other possible signs of infection: Seek urgent GP or urgent-care advice for severe joint pain that started suddenly, usually in one joint. Swelling around a joint, changed skin colour or difficulty moving the joint also need urgent advice. Joint pain with fever, shivering or feeling unwell also needs urgent advice. These signs do not all need to occur together. Do not wait for a fever. Use 111 where available, or your local urgent-care route in Northern Ireland. Call 999 for life-threatening symptoms.
  • After a fall or injury: go to A&E or call 999 for very bad joint pain, inability to walk or put weight on a joint, a joint out of place, or tingling or loss of feeling around the joint. Do not drive yourself.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team urgently for signs of infection while taking immune-suppressing medicines. Use your local urgent-care service if they are unavailable.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team if a flare is not settling in the time agreed with your clinician or you are struggling to cope. Book a GP appointment if flares are becoming more frequent or you have never been given a diagnosis for your joint pain.

England: NHS 111. Scotland: NHS 24 on 111, with your own GP the usual route for urgent advice during normal working hours. Wales: NHS 111 Wales. Northern Ireland: contact your GP or local GP out-of-hours service; Phone First is available in some Trust areas.

faqs.q: Is there a free printable arthritis flare action plan?
faqs.a: Yes. The plan on this page is free to print or save as a PDF from your browser's print window. Fill in the medicines section with your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team, and keep a copy where you and the people who help you can find it.

faqs.q: What should I do first when my arthritis flares?
faqs.a: Check for red flag signs first. If there are none, follow your plan: reduce activity for a short time while keeping gently mobile, use cold on hot swollen joints or warmth on stiff ones, take only medicines your clinician has agreed, pace your day and start tracking symptoms.

faqs.q: How long should I manage a flare at home before getting help?
faqs.a: It depends on your type of arthritis and treatment, so ask your GP or rheumatology team to agree a timescale and write it in your plan. Get help sooner if you have any red flag signs, if symptoms are getting worse rather than better, or if you are not coping.

faqs.q: Should I rest completely during an arthritis flare?
faqs.a: Usually not. A short rest for a very painful joint is reasonable, but long periods without moving tend to make stiffness and weakness worse. Gentle movement through a comfortable range, little and often, usually helps more than staying still all day.

faqs.q: Can I change my arthritis medicines during a flare?
faqs.a: Only if your clinician has agreed it. Do not stop or double regular arthritis medicines yourself, and never stop steroid tablets suddenly. Ask your pharmacist about over-the-counter options and your specialist team about a flare plan for inflammatory arthritis.

faqs.q: Who should have a copy of my flare action plan?
faqs.a: You, and anyone who helps you during a flare, such as a partner, family member or carer. Some people also bring it to GP, rheumatology or physiotherapy appointments so their team can see what has been agreed and suggest changes.

/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.title: Mediterranean vs Anti-Inflammatory Diet for Arthritis
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.description: Compare Mediterranean and 'anti-inflammatory' diets for arthritis: NICE advice, uncertain symptom benefits, balanced meals and supplement safety.
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.question: Is the Mediterranean diet the same as an anti-inflammatory diet?
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.answer: No. A Mediterranean-style diet is an eating pattern based on vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, nuts and unsaturated oils. 'Anti-inflammatory diet' is a broad label without one agreed definition. NICE says there is no strong evidence that changing diet will benefit rheumatoid arthritis, although Mediterranean principles can be encouraged. Food changes do not replace arthritis treatment.

faqs.q: Which eating pattern should I choose?
faqs.a: Choose a balanced, affordable pattern you can sustain and adapt to your needs. Mediterranean principles are one option. NICE advises explaining the uncertainty about arthritis benefit rather than promising pain relief.

faqs.q: Should I try an elimination diet or supplements?
faqs.a: Not routinely for arthritis. Discuss a proposed exclusion with a registered dietitian and check supplements with a pharmacist or your healthcare team. Follow specific advice for a diagnosed allergy, coeliac disease or another condition.

faqs.q: How long before my arthritis improves?
faqs.a: There is no reliable time-to-benefit promise for either label. Continue your arthritis treatment and seek a review for persistent or worsening symptoms rather than waiting for a diet to work.

/guides/shoulder-pain-relief.title: Shoulder pain: safe self-care and when to get help
/guides/shoulder-pain-relief.description: Keep a painful shoulder moving gently, but avoid movements that aggravate it. A pharmacist can advise on suitable pain relief. Arrange GP review if pain is
/guides/shoulder-pain-relief.answer: Keep a painful shoulder moving gently, but avoid movements that aggravate it. A pharmacist can advise on suitable pain relief. Arrange GP review if pain is worsening or has not started improving after two weeks. Sudden severe pain, inability to move the arm, injury, marked swelling, persistent pins and needles or feeling feverish need urgent assessment.
/guides/shoulder-pain-relief.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

Keep a painful shoulder moving gently, but avoid movements that aggravate it. A pharmacist can advise on suitable pain relief. Arrange GP review if pain is worsening or has not started improving after two weeks. Sudden severe pain, inability to move the arm, injury, marked swelling, persistent pins and needles or feeling feverish need urgent assessment.

When to get urgent help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if pain is sudden or very severe, you cannot move the arm, the shoulder changes shape or becomes badly swollen, pins and needles do not settle, sensation is lost, the arm feels unusually hot or cold, symptoms follow an injury, both shoulders become severely painful, or you feel feverish or unwell. Do not treat these as an ordinary exercise flare.

What you can try

Use comfortable, gentle shoulder movements rather than stopping all movement. Support the arm on a cushion when sitting if that helps. You can try a wrapped warm or cold pack for comfort, following NHS guidance and protecting the skin. Avoid activities that make symptoms worse, heavy gym equipment and a strenuous routine you have devised yourself.

Pain relief is individual

Ask a pharmacist which pain relief is suitable for you, particularly if you take other medicines or have another health condition. Products differ, so follow the label and professional advice rather than a universal application schedule. This guide does not prescribe a medicine or dose.

Exercise and recovery

There is no single routine or pain score suitable for every shoulder problem. Start with gentle movement and ask a physiotherapist for an appropriate programme if needed. Recovery varies and can take months. Do not force through severe pain or use a promised recovery deadline to decide whether assessment is needed.

Arrange a review

See a GP if symptoms worsen, do not start improving after two weeks, or movement is very difficult. In many areas you may be able to refer yourself to an NHS musculoskeletal service. Availability and referral routes vary locally.

Frequently asked questions

Should I rest completely? Usually not. Keep comfortable movement, but do not persist with activities that worsen symptoms. Urgent symptoms need assessment rather than self-management.

Is a pain score of 4/10 always safe? No universal threshold is given here. Your symptoms, diagnosis and agreed rehabilitation plan matter.

Do I need to wait six weeks before seeing a GP? No. NHS advice is to seek review if worsening or not improving after two weeks, with earlier urgent help for the symptoms above.

/blog/signs-rheumatoid-arthritis-early-s.title: Early rheumatoid arthritis: signs and getting assessed
/blog/signs-rheumatoid-arthritis-early-s.description: Rheumatoid arthritis can begin with painful, swollen joints, stiffness after rest and tiredness. Small joints in the hands and feet are often affected, but
/blog/signs-rheumatoid-arthritis-early-s.answer: Rheumatoid arthritis can begin with painful, swollen joints, stiffness after rest and tiredness. Small joints in the hands and feet are often affected, but symptoms differ. Persistent unexplained joint swelling needs prompt assessment. A GP can arrange tests and refer to rheumatology; blood tests should not hold up an urgent referral.
/blog/signs-rheumatoid-arthritis-early-s.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

Rheumatoid arthritis can begin with painful, swollen joints, stiffness after rest and tiredness. Small joints in the hands and feet are often affected, but symptoms differ. Persistent unexplained joint swelling needs prompt assessment. A GP can arrange tests and refer to rheumatology; blood tests should not hold up an urgent referral.

What to notice

Joint pain, swelling and stiffness may develop over weeks, although symptoms sometimes begin more quickly. Both sides of the body can be affected, but a perfectly symmetrical pattern is not required. Fatigue and feeling generally unwell can accompany joint symptoms. These signs do not establish a diagnosis by themselves.

What to tell the GP

Explain which joints are swollen, when symptoms began, how mornings and daily tasks are affected, and whether symptoms come and go. Mention symptoms even if pain is manageable or you have had a normal blood test. NICE recommends urgent specialist referral for persistent synovitis when small hand or foot joints, or more than one joint, are affected; delay in seeking help is another reason for urgency.

What three working days means

NICE quality standard QS33 sets a target for referral within three working days of presentation in primary care for suspected persistent synovitis affecting multiple joints or the small joints of the hands and feet. That is the referral target, not a guarantee that the specialist appointment will take place within three days. Do not wait six weeks before reporting persistent swelling.

While assessment is arranged

Ask your GP what pain relief and activity are suitable and how to seek help if symptoms change. Keep a short symptom record if useful. Do not start or stop prescription treatment based on this page. A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint, especially with illness or shivering, needs urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

/blog/giant-cell-arteritis-headache-warn.title: Giant cell arteritis: urgent symptoms and assessment
/blog/giant-cell-arteritis-headache-warn.description: Giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, is inflammation of arteries that can threaten sight. If you think you may have it, ask for an urgent
/blog/giant-cell-arteritis-headache-warn.answer: Giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, is inflammation of arteries that can threaten sight. If you think you may have it, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. Do not wait for a routine headache appointment. If you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes, or have sudden severe eye pain, go to A&E or call 999. Do not drive yourself.
/blog/giant-cell-arteritis-headache-warn.bodyHtml:
Get help promptly

Giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, is inflammation of arteries that can threaten sight. If you think you may have it, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. Do not wait for a routine headache appointment. If you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes, or have sudden severe eye pain, go to A&E or call 999. Do not drive yourself.

Symptoms to explain

Tell the clinician about a new or severe headache, tenderness at the temples or scalp, jaw pain when chewing or talking, and any change in vision. Tiredness, weight loss and flu-like symptoms can also occur. Symptoms overlap with other conditions, so this page cannot diagnose the cause.

Vision changes need urgent attention

Blurred or double vision, a dark shadow or other new visual changes need urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment. Tell them if these occur with headache, scalp tenderness or jaw pain. NHS temporal-arteritis guidance says people with vision problems should have a same-day hospital eye-specialist appointment. Sudden inability to see or sudden severe eye pain uses the emergency route above.

What assessment may involve

A clinician may examine you, arrange blood tests and refer you for specialist assessment. Ultrasound of the temporal arteries or a biopsy may be used. Because delayed treatment can risk sight, clinicians may begin steroid treatment before the diagnosis is fully confirmed.

Treatment and follow-up

Treatment commonly involves prednisolone with a plan to reduce it under supervision. Follow-up checks both the disease and treatment side effects. Do not suddenly stop prescribed steroids. Ask your team whom to contact if symptoms return or new vision symptoms appear.

/blog/septic-arthritis-hot-swollen-joint.title: A suddenly painful, swollen joint: urgent help
/blog/septic-arthritis-hot-swollen-joint.description: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for a suddenly very painful joint, swelling, skin colour change, difficulty moving it, or joint pain wi
/blog/septic-arthritis-hot-swollen-joint.answer: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for a suddenly very painful joint, swelling, skin colour change, difficulty moving it, or joint pain with feeling unwell, fever or shivering. Septic arthritis is a joint infection needing prompt treatment. Fever is not always present, so do not wait for it.
/blog/septic-arthritis-hot-swollen-joint.bodyHtml:
Get urgent help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for a suddenly very painful joint, swelling, skin colour change, difficulty moving it, or joint pain with feeling unwell, fever or shivering. Septic arthritis is a joint infection needing prompt treatment. Fever is not always present, so do not wait for it.

When to call 999

Call 999 or go to A&E if you think someone has sepsis with signs such as confusion or slurred speech, severe breathlessness or very fast breathing, or blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin. A rash that does not fade under a glass is another emergency sign. Do not wait for every symptom, and do not drive yourself to A&E.

Why prompt assessment matters

Symptoms can develop quickly. Gout, injury and other illnesses may also cause a hot or swollen joint, but you cannot reliably distinguish them at home. Explain when symptoms started and whether you have a joint replacement, recent surgery, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis or medicines that affect immunity.

What treatment may involve

People with septic arthritis are usually treated in hospital. Treatment may include antibiotics into a vein and drainage of fluid from the joint, followed by antibiotic tablets. The team decides which tests and procedures are needed. Finish prescribed antibiotics for the duration you are told, even if symptoms improve.

After hospital treatment

Follow the discharge and follow-up plan. Physiotherapy may help movement return as recovery allows. A joint replacement infection can need a different surgical plan. Seek advice promptly if you worsen or symptoms return rather than relying on an expected recovery timetable.

/blog/best-plantar-fasciitis-shoes-women.title: Shoes for plantar fasciitis: a practical fit guide
/blog/best-plantar-fasciitis-shoes-women.description: For plantar-fasciitis heel or arch pain, NHS advice favours cushioned heels and good arch support. A shoe should fit comfortably rather than squeeze the to
/blog/best-plantar-fasciitis-shoes-women.answer: For plantar-fasciitis heel or arch pain, NHS advice favours cushioned heels and good arch support. A shoe should fit comfortably rather than squeeze the toes or rub the heel. There is no verified best brand in this guide. A pharmacist or podiatrist can help if you need advice about insoles, pads or suitable footwear.
/blog/best-plantar-fasciitis-shoes-women.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

For plantar-fasciitis heel or arch pain, NHS advice favours cushioned heels and good arch support. A shoe should fit comfortably rather than squeeze the toes or rub the heel. There is no verified best brand in this guide. A pharmacist or podiatrist can help if you need advice about insoles, pads or suitable footwear.

What to look for

Use cushioning and arch support as starting points, then check how the shoe feels on your own foot. NHS guidance advises against high heels, tight pointed shoes, flip-flops and backless slippers. Avoid walking barefoot on hard surfaces if it worsens symptoms. A higher price or a medical-looking label is not proof that a shoe suits you.

A practical try-on

Try the shoes with the socks or prescribed insoles you intend to wear. Check for pressure, rubbing and heel slippage during a short indoor walk. This is a practical shopping check, not a validated medical test or a promise of pain relief. Check the retailer return terms before wearing shoes outdoors.

Shoes are only part of care

NHS self-care also includes reducing prolonged standing or walking, gentle foot and heel stretches, and activities that place less pressure on the feet, such as swimming. A pharmacist can advise about suitable pain relief and pads. Do not use footwear changes as a reason to ignore persistent symptoms.

When to seek help

See a GP if pain is severe, limits normal activities, worsens or keeps returning, or has not improved after two weeks of self-care. Tingling, loss of feeling, or foot pain when you have diabetes also warrant medical advice. Physiotherapy or podiatry may be considered when symptoms persist; local access and waiting times vary.

About women-specific claims

This page does not claim that a particular women-branded shoe treats plantar fasciitis better. Choose by comfort, fit, cushioning and support, with individual advice when needed. No current stock, prices or product endorsements are asserted.

/conditions/osteoarthritis.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

Osteoarthritis affects the tissues of a joint and can cause pain, stiffness and difficulty with movement. It commonly affects knees, hips and hands. Treatment is tailored to your needs; exercise and, where relevant, weight management are central parts of care. Medicines, aids or surgery may be considered when appropriate.

Recognising symptoms

Pain and stiffness vary from person to person. Symptoms may affect activity, work or everyday tasks, but pain alone does not confirm osteoarthritis. Ask a GP about persistent or worrying joint symptoms. A sudden very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment rather than assuming it is your usual arthritis.

How it is assessed

NICE says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed clinically in people aged 45 or over who have activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes. Imaging is not routinely needed for diagnosis unless there are atypical features or another diagnosis is suspected. Your clinician decides what applies to you.

Treatment starts with an individual plan

NICE recommends tailored therapeutic exercise, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. Some discomfort can occur when starting, but an appropriate regular programme can improve pain, function and quality of life over time. Ask for help adapting activity if you are unsure. If living with overweight or obesity, supported weight management can help symptoms and function.

Medicines and other options

If medicine is needed, the choice depends on the joint, other health conditions and other medicines. NICE recommends a topical NSAID for knee osteoarthritis and considers it for other joints. Oral NSAIDs require an individual risk assessment. Do not select a medicine or dose from this summary; ask a pharmacist or clinician. Aids, physiotherapy and, in some cases, joint-replacement assessment may be discussed.

Where to go next

Use the arthritis overview to understand different diagnoses, the daily-living guide for practical adjustments, and the UK care guide to plan an appointment. This page does not use an older treatment-seeking estimate as a current count of everyone with osteoarthritis.

/guides/uk-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Quick answer

Start with a GP assessment for unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not settle. Sudden severe symptoms may need urgent help. The next step depends on the suspected condition: some people need rheumatology, others may benefit from physiotherapy or occupational therapy. Referral routes and services vary across the UK.

Choose the right route

For a suddenly very painful, swollen or hot joint, or joint symptoms with fever, shivering or feeling unwell, ask for urgent GP help or contact NHS 111. Otherwise, arrange GP review for unexplained pain, swelling or stiffness that persists beyond a few days. This guide is for navigation, not diagnosis.

Prepare for the appointment

Note which joints are affected, when symptoms began, whether swelling comes and goes, how long stiffness lasts and which tasks are harder. Bring a current medicine list and explain your main concern. Ask what the likely diagnosis is, whether tests are needed, and what to do if symptoms worsen.

Understand a referral

NICE recommends urgent rheumatology referral for suspected persistent synovitis with specified features, including small hand or foot joints or more than one joint. QS33 sets a three-working-day referral target for these groups; it is not a guaranteed appointment within three days. Blood tests should not delay an urgent referral.

Rehabilitation and daily tasks

In many areas you can approach an NHS musculoskeletal service without a GP referral, but check local arrangements. Physiotherapy can support movement and strength; occupational therapy can help with everyday activities and equipment. Ask your team which service fits your needs rather than assuming every area offers the same route.

Leave with a plan

Before the appointment ends, ask who will arrange tests or referrals, how results will reach you, when review is due and whom to contact if you deteriorate. For medicine questions, ask your pharmacist or prescribing team. For an explanation of arthritis types use the overview; for adapting daily life use the daily-living guide.
